Each value can be set only once, even with the same content. Every setting is checked before the instance folder is created, so an invalid setting leaves nothing behind. A setting has the form ADDRESS=VALUE, where ADDRESS names what to set in one of three ways. By placeholder category: Config files hold placeholders such as '${{literal:tdk_database_host}}' or '${{secret:postgres_system_password}}'. The word before the colon is the placeholder kind (literal, literalAuto, secret or secretAuto can be set), and the word after it is the category. Naming the category sets every placeholder of that category, in every config file at once: tdk_database_host=db.internal The kind can be prefixed to the category, and it must be when two kinds share one category: secret:postgres_system_user=tabsdata By file and key path: Any final value of a config file, placeholder or not, is addressed by the file name (with or without '.yaml'), a colon, and the path of keys down to the value, joined by dots: tabsdata:pods.service.resources.cpu=4 A list item is selected by its position, starting at 0, or by the value of one of its keys: tabsdata:pods.service.placement.tolerations[0].effect=NoExecute tabsdata:pods.service.placement.tolerations[operator=Exists].effect=NoExecute A key that contains dots is quoted, as in 'section."key.with.dots".value'. From a settings file: '@FILE' reads settings from a YAML file. It may be a list of 'ADDRESS=VALUE' strings, a mapping of addresses to values, or a mapping with two sections: 'files', with the keys of each config file nested as in the file itself, and 'values', a mapping of addresses to values: files: tabsdata: pods: service: resources: cpu: "4" values: tdk_database_host: db.internal secret:postgres_system_password: env:POSTGRES_PASSWORD Only values that already exist can be set: never new keys, and never a key that holds other keys or a list. There are two exceptions. New environment variables can be added under 'tabsdata:pods.global.envs' for every pod and function: tabsdata:pods.global.envs.MY_API_KEY=env:MY_API_KEY and new keys can be added to any mapping its config schema declares open, such as the 'options' of a storage mount: apiserver.storage:storage.mounts[id=ROOT].options.aws_region=eu-west-1 A value the schema declares secret can be set even where it holds a placeholder the system resolves, such as the 'uri' of a kminus storage mount. Their values are written as strings. A string value replaces a string, while numbers and booleans replace only values of their own type. A VALUE starting with 'env:' is read from that environment variable of this machine, so secrets need not be written in any file of yours. To combine variables with fixed text, wrap each variable in '${...}': 'env:${BUCKET_URI}/root' reads BUCKET_URI and appends '/root'. 'val:' keeps a value that literally starts with 'env:'. Secret values end up in the instance input config files. By placeholder category: Config files hold placeholders such as '${{literal:tdk_database_host}}' or '${{secret:postgres_system_password}}'. The word before the colon is the placeholder kind (literal, literalAuto, secret or secretAuto can be set), and the word after it is the category. Naming the category sets every placeholder of that category, in every config file at once: tdk_database_host=db.internal The kind can be prefixed to the category, and it must be when two kinds share one category: secret:postgres_system_user=tabsdata By file and key path: Any final value of a config file, placeholder or not, is addressed by the file name (with or without '.yaml'), a colon, and the path of keys down to the value, joined by dots: tabsdata:pods.service.resources.cpu=4 A list item is selected by its position, starting at 0, or by the value of one of its keys: tabsdata:pods.service.placement.tolerations[0].effect=NoExecute tabsdata:pods.service.placement.tolerations[operator=Exists].effect=NoExecute A key that contains dots is quoted, as in 'section."key.with.dots".value'. From a settings file: '@FILE' reads settings from a YAML file. It may be a list of 'ADDRESS=VALUE' strings, a mapping of addresses to values, or a mapping with two sections: 'files', with the keys of each config file nested as in the file itself, and 'values', a mapping of addresses to values: files: tabsdata: pods: service: resources: cpu: "4" values: tdk_database_host: db.internal secret:postgres_system_password: env:POSTGRES_PASSWORD Only values that already exist can be set: never new keys, and never a key that holds other keys or a list. There are two exceptions. New environment variables can be added under 'tabsdata:pods.global.envs' for every pod and function: tabsdata:pods.global.envs.MY_API_KEY=env:MY_API_KEY and new keys can be added to any mapping its config schema declares open, such as the 'options' of a storage mount: apiserver.storage:storage.mounts[id=ROOT].options.aws_region=eu-west-1 A value the schema declares secret can be set even where it holds a placeholder the system resolves, such as the 'uri' of a kminus storage mount. Their values are written as strings. A string value replaces a string, while numbers and booleans replace only values of their own type. A VALUE starting with 'env:' is read from that environment variable of this machine, so secrets need not be written in any file of yours. To combine variables with fixed text, wrap each variable in '${...}': 'env:${BUCKET_URI}/root' reads BUCKET_URI and appends '/root'. 'val:' keeps a value that literally starts with 'env:'. Secret values end up in the instance input config files. Examples: tdkserver init --provider gke --config tdk_database_host=db.internal --config secret:postgres_system_password=env:POSTGRES_PASSWORD tdkserver quickstart --config tabsdata:pods.service.resources.memory=8Gi tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY tdkserver quickstart --config tabsdata:pods.global.envs.MY_API_KEY=env:MY_API_KEY tdkserver quickstart --config @settings.yaml --requirements string Optional Complementary packages for every tabsdata base virtual environment, in pip requirements format. The file is checked to be a valid pip requirements file before the instance folder is created, and its requirements are added to the requirements-*.txt init assets of the new instance, after the ones those already hold, so the virtual environments are built with them when the instance is created. Nothing else is checked: a package that cannot be installed fails the creation. Example: tdkserver quickstart --requirements drivers.txt --fill flag Optional Fill the configuration stub of the provider in a built-in editor before anything is created. The editor opens the stub of the chosen provider, or the file left by an earlier '--fill' of the same instance, with the required values marked. Ctrl+Q saves and continues once the settings are valid, Ctrl+S saves without leaving, and Esc quits without saving, which cancels the quickstart. Editing keys use Ctrl, also on macOS: the terminal keeps Cmd for itself. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X and Ctrl+V use the system clipboard, so text moves between the editor and other applications, and Cmd+V pastes too. Ctrl+A selects all; Shift with the arrows, or a mouse drag, selects a block. The filled file is used as '--config @FILE', together with any other '--config' settings, and it is kept in the 'init/fill' folder of the instance.
